result.markdown: --- title: "Session 2 — Simple Methods and Why They Fail" subtitle: "Complete case · mean imputation · missing indicator · single imputation · Lab 2" author: "Community Medicine Workshop" format: revealjs: theme: serif css: [../assets/slide_deck.css, assets/workshop.css, assets/quiz.css] include-after-body: assets/quiz-include.html embed-resources: true slide-number: true navigation-mode: linear code-copy: true center: false transition: fade width: 1280 height: 720 fig-align: center html-math-method: plain execute: echo: true warning: false message: false fig-width: 9 fig-height: 4.6 fig-dpi: 100 --- ## Where we are ::: {.incremental} - Session 1: the amount, pattern and mechanism of missingness - Today: the **simple fixes** that people still use, and what goes wrong - The question: how does **BMI** relate to **SBP**? (true coefficient about **0.80 mmHg per BMI unit**) - By the end you can: - explain the **bias** and **variance** problems of each simple method - see why a **single imputation** gives SEs that are **too small** ::: # Topic 1 — Complete-case analysis {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Listwise deletion ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m_cc <- lm(sbp ~ age + sex + bmi + smoker + activity, data = dat) c(adults_used = nobs(m_cc), of = nrow(dat)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` adults_used of 1101 2000 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} round(summary(m_cc)$coefficients["bmi", ], 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) 0.685 0.071 9.609 0.000 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.key} `lm()` silently drops incomplete rows: **1,101 of 2,000** adults are used. The BMI coefficient is **0.685** (SE 0.071): **too low** (truth about 0.80). BMI is missing more often when **SBP is high**, so the adults who remain have **lower SBP at a given BMI**: the slope is **attenuated**. ::: ::: {.warn} Complete-case is valid under **MCAR**, and under some **MAR** conditions. Here the missingness depends on the **outcome**: biased. ::: # Topic 2 — Single fixes {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Mean imputation ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} d_mean <- dat |> mutate(bmi_m = ifelse(is.na(bmi), mean(bmi, na.rm = TRUE), bmi)) c(before = sd(dat$bmi, na.rm = TRUE), after = sd(d_mean$bmi_m)) |> round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` before after 4.32 3.71 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} m_mean <- lm(sbp ~ age + sex + bmi_m + smoker + activity, data = d_mean) round(summary(m_mean)$coefficients["bmi_m", 1:2], 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error 0.697 0.079 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - SD falls from **4.3 to 3.7**: a quarter of the adults sit **exactly at the mean** - The coefficient stays **biased** (0.70) and the SE (0.079) is **not valid** - **Weakens correlations**, distorts distributions - Do **not** use it ::: ## Missing-indicator method ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} d_ind <- dat |> mutate(bmi_miss = as.integer(is.na(bmi)), bmi0 = ifelse(is.na(bmi), 0, bmi)) m_ind <- lm(sbp ~ age + sex + bmi0 + bmi_miss + smoker + activity, data = d_ind) round(summary(m_ind)$coefficients[c("bmi0", "bmi_miss"), 1:2], 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error bmi0 0.684 0.071 bmi_miss 28.146 1.812 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.warn} BMI coefficient **0.68** (still biased). The indicator absorbs a huge "effect" of **28 mmHg**: an **artefact** of filling missing BMI with 0. The method is **biased even when data are MAR**. ::: ## Single stochastic imputation ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} imp1 <- mice(dat, m = 1, maxit = 10, seed = 1, printFlag = FALSE) m_single <- lm(sbp ~ age + sex + bmi + smoker + activity, data = complete(imp1)) round(summary(m_single)$coefficients["bmi", 1:2], 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error 0.750 0.057 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.key} Imputing **with noise, using SBP**, moves the estimate to **0.75**. But the **SE is 0.057**: **smaller than the complete-case SE** (0.071) although **a quarter of the BMI values were invented**. A single imputation treats made-up values as **real data**. ::: ## Comparison ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tibble(method = c("complete case", "mean imputation", "missing indicator", "single imputation"), estimate = c(coef(m_cc)[["bmi"]], coef(m_mean)[["bmi_m"]], coef(m_ind)[["bmi0"]], coef(m_single)[["bmi"]]), se = c(summary(m_cc)$coefficients["bmi", 2], summary(m_mean)$coefficients["bmi_m", 2], summary(m_ind)$coefficients["bmi0", 2], summary(m_single)$coefficients["bmi", 2])) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 3 method estimate se 1 complete case 0.685 0.071 2 mean imputation 0.697 0.079 3 missing indicator 0.684 0.071 4 single imputation 0.75 0.057 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - Complete-case, mean and indicator: **biased** (0.68 to 0.70 vs about 0.80) - Mean imputation and single imputation: **wrong SEs** - We need a method that **adds noise to the imputed values** **and** **reflects the uncertainty** in the SE: **multiple imputation** (Session 3) ::: ## 🔧 Switch to R — Lab 2 {.lab-slide background-color="#1565c0"} ::: {.lab-box} **File:** `missing-workshop/labs/lab2_simple.R` - complete-case model and number of adults used - mean imputation and its SD - missing indicator, single imputation, comparison table ::: **Time:** 35 minutes · answer the Q questions in the comments ## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="m2q1" data-type="mcq" data-hash="mf8ym2.sgup9g" data-show="VGhlIGltcHV0ZWQgdmFsdWVzIGFsbCBzaXQgYXQgdGhlIG1lYW4sIHNvIHRoZSBzcHJlYWQg b2YgdGhlIHZhcmlhYmxlIHNocmlua3M=" data-explain="QSBxdWFydGVyIG9mIHRoZSBhZHVsdHMgZ2V0IGV4YWN0bHkgdGhlIHNhbWUgdmFsdWUuIFRo YXQgYWRkcyBubyBzcHJlYWQsIHNvIHRoZSB2YXJpYW5jZSBmYWxscywgY29ycmVsYXRpb25z IHdlYWtlbiBhbmQgdGhlIFNFcyBhcmUgd3Jvbmcu"} Mean imputation reduces the SD of BMI from 4.3 to 3.7. Why? - The imputed values are drawn from a narrower distribution than the observed ones - The imputed values all sit at the mean, so the spread of the variable shrinks - Mean imputation removes the adults with extreme BMI values from the sample - The mean is estimated from fewer adults than the standard deviation is ::: ## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="m2q2" data-type="mcq" data-hash="mf9but.sgv3qv" data-show="SXQgaXMgYW4gYXJ0ZWZhY3Qgb2YgZmlsbGluZyBtaXNzaW5nIEJNSSB3aXRoIDAsIG5vdCBh IHJlYWwgZWZmZWN0" data-explain="U2V0dGluZyBCTUkgdG8gMCBtYWtlcyB0aGUgaW5kaWNhdG9yIGFic29yYiB0aGUgZ2FwIGJl dHdlZW4gMCBhbmQgdGhlIHRydWUgQk1JLCBzbyB0aGUgbGFyZ2UgY29lZmZpY2llbnQgaXMg Y3JlYXRlZCBieSB0aGUgbWV0aG9kLg=="} In the missing-indicator method the indicator has a coefficient of 28 mmHg. How should this be read? - Adults with a missing BMI truly have an SBP 28 mmHg higher than the others - It shows that the data are missing not at random for BMI in the cohort - It is the amount of bias that the complete-case analysis has - It is an artefact of filling missing BMI with 0, not a real effect ::: ## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="m2q3" data-type="mcq" data-hash="mf9p3f.sgvi85" data-show="VGhlIGltcHV0ZWQgdmFsdWVzIGFyZSB0cmVhdGVkIGFzIGlmIHRoZXkgaGFkIGJlZW4gb2Jz ZXJ2ZWQ=" data-explain="QSBzaW5nbGUgY29tcGxldGVkIGRhdGEgc2V0IGhpZGVzIHRoZSB1bmNlcnRhaW50eSBhYm91 dCB0aGUgaW1wdXRlZCB2YWx1ZXMsIHNvIGFuYWx5c2lzIHNvZnR3YXJlIGNvdW50cyB0aGVt IGFzIHJlYWwgb2JzZXJ2YXRpb25zIGFuZCB1bmRlcnN0YXRlcyB0aGUgU0Uu"} A single stochastic imputation gives an SE of 0.057, below the complete-case SE of 0.071, although a quarter of BMI is imputed. Why? - The imputed values are treated as if they had been observed - Imputation increases the sample size, so the SE must fall - The SE from a stochastic imputation is too large, not too small - The model has more predictors after the BMI values are imputed ::: ## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="m2q4" data-type="mcq" data-hash="mfa2c6.sgvwpk" data-show="V2hlbiBtaXNzaW5nbmVzcyBkb2VzIG5vdCBkZXBlbmQgb24gdGhlIG91dGNvbWUsIGdpdmVu IHRoZSBjb3ZhcmlhdGVz" data-explain="SWYgbWlzc2luZ25lc3MgZG9lcyBub3QgZGVwZW5kIG9uIHRoZSBvdXRjb21lIG9uY2UgdGhl IG1vZGVsIGNvdmFyaWF0ZXMgYXJlIGFjY291bnRlZCBmb3IsIHRoZSByZW1haW5pbmcgYWR1 bHRzIGdpdmUgdmFsaWQgcmVncmVzc2lvbiBlc3RpbWF0ZXMuIEhlcmUgaXQgZGVwZW5kZWQg b24gU0JQLCBzbyBpdCBmYWlsZWQu"} When is a complete-case analysis expected to be unbiased? - When more than 5% of the values of the variable are missing in the data set - When the incomplete variable is continuous and has a roughly normal shape in the sample - When missingness does not depend on the outcome, given the covariates - When the data are missing at random for the variables in the dataset ::: ## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="m2q5" data-type="mcq" data-hash="mfafku.sgwb6w" data-show="VGhleSBsb3NlIGRhdGEsIGJpYXMgdGhlIGVzdGltYXRlcywgb3IgZ2l2ZSBTRXMgdGhhdCBh cmUgdG9vIHNtYWxs" data-explain="RWFjaCBzaW1wbGUgbWV0aG9kIGZhaWxzIGluIGF0IGxlYXN0IG9uZSB3YXk6IGRlbGV0aW9u IGxvc2VzIGRhdGEgYW5kIG1heSBiaWFzLCBtZWFuIGFuZCBpbmRpY2F0b3IgbWV0aG9kcyBi aWFzLCBhbmQgc2luZ2xlIGltcHV0YXRpb24gdW5kZXJzdGF0ZXMgdGhlIFNFLg=="} What is the fair summary of the simple methods? - They are as good as multiple imputation when under 30% of values are missing - They lose data, bias the estimates, or give SEs that are too small - They are valid for MAR data but not for MCAR data in a regression model - They fail when the outcome variable is the one that has missing values ::: ## Score and take-home **Your score: ** ::: {.incremental} - **Complete-case**: loses data, biased if missingness depends on the outcome - **Mean imputation**: shrinks variance, biased, wrong SE - **Missing indicator**: biased even under MAR - **Single imputation**: SE too small (imputed = real) - Need **multiple** imputation ::: **Next:** Session 3: multiple imputation with mice

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
